title: Buffett's Preferred Vanguard S&P 500 ETF Turns $10,000 Into Over $42,000 in 12 Years
excerpt: Warren Buffett has championed the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF since 2014, and the numbers have vindicated his advice — with the fund delivering nearly 13% annual returns and outperforming the vast majority of professional fund managers.
body:
• The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO), which Buffett recommended in his 2013 shareholder letter, has turned a $10,000 investment into roughly $42,887 since 2014 — a compound annual return of 12.9%.
  • Nearly 87% of actively managed large-cap funds underperformed the S&P 500 over five years, and 91% lagged over 20 years, according to the SPIVA Scorecard.
  • VOO charges an expense ratio of just 0.03% — or $3 annually per $10,000 invested — making it one of the cheapest ways to own the 500 largest U.S. companies.
  • For Indian diaspora investors balancing portfolios across markets, the fund offers diversified U.S. exposure without the complexity of stock-picking.

Warren Buffett built his $149 billion fortune picking individual stocks, but his advice for everyone else has been strikingly simple: buy a low-cost S&P 500 index fund and hold it for the long term.

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) — the specific fund Buffett has endorsed repeatedly since 2013 — has proven him right. An investor who put $10,000 into the fund when Buffett first recommended it would be sitting on approximately $42,887 today, a return of nearly 329%, according to analysis by The Motley Fool.

The Three-Word Endorsement

Buffett's clearest endorsement came in his 2013 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, where he revealed the instructions in his will for the money his wife would inherit.

"Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. I suggest Vanguard's."

— Warren Buffett, 2013 Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder Letter

Those three words — "I suggest Vanguard's" — amounted to one of the most consequential fund endorsements in investing history. Berkshire Hathaway itself holds positions in both the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY), though its Vanguard stake is slightly larger at $21.5 million.

At Berkshire's 2020 annual meeting, Buffett reiterated: "For most people, the best thing to do is to own the S&P 500 index fund." At a subsequent meeting, he added practical advice: "Just pick a broad index like the S&P 500. Don't put your money in all at once; do it over a period of time."

The Numbers Behind the Advice

The S&P 500 has delivered a compound annual return of roughly 10.5% since its establishment in 1957. But since Buffett's recommendation in 2014, the pace has been even faster — 12.9% per year — fueled by rapid growth in cloud computing, enterprise software, and artificial intelligence.

VOO's appeal extends beyond returns. The fund charges an expense ratio of just 0.03%, meaning investors pay only $3 per year for every $10,000 invested. That compares to an industry average of 0.72% for similar funds, according to Vanguard. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, the other fund Berkshire owns, charges 0.0945%.

The case for passive investing over professional management is now well documented. According to S&P Global's SPIVA Scorecard, 86.9% of large-cap stock funds underperformed the S&P 500 over five years after accounting for fees. Over 20 years, that figure climbs to 91%.

"By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

— Warren Buffett, 1993 Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder Letter

VOO has grown into one of the largest investment funds in the world, with assets exceeding $950 billion. Q1 2026 S&P 500 earnings grew by roughly 28% year over year, the strongest result since 2021, buoyed by AI-driven gains in the technology sector.

What It Means for Diaspora Investors

For Indian Americans and NRIs managing investments across multiple markets, Buffett's framework offers a practical anchor for U.S. equity allocation. Rather than navigating the complexity of individual stock selection in an unfamiliar market, a single VOO position provides exposure to 500 of the largest American companies spanning technology, healthcare, financials, and consumer goods — all for a fee that amounts to a rounding error.

The strategy also pairs well with existing holdings in Indian equities, offering geographic diversification without the need for active management on the U.S. side.

What's Next

Buffett stepped down as Berkshire Hathaway CEO in 2025, but his investing philosophy endures. The technologies he cited as future growth drivers — artificial intelligence, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and quantum computing — remain in early stages and could continue propelling S&P 500 gains for years.

For investors who missed the 2014 entry point, analysts note the advice remains relevant. At its current pace, $500 invested monthly in VOO could grow to roughly $1 million over 30 years, assuming the index maintains its historical average return of about 10.4% annually.

As Buffett wrote more than a decade ago, the combination of low cost and broad diversification is "virtually certain to get satisfactory results." Twelve years of data suggest that assessment was, if anything, conservative.
